overview: This file combines a 1947 State Department policy packet on the disposition of Japanese merchant vessels as reparations with 1948 material concerning the future size and trading scope of Japan’s merchant marine. The earlier documents recommend abandoning the U.S. formula for allocating ships according to wartime losses, because the revised reparations pool—perhaps only eleven ships totaling about 100,000 gross tons—was too small to justify a contentious distribution policy; they include correspondence, internal clearances, a comparative policy paper, and a vessel-by-vessel estimate. The later documents record official discussion of whether Japanese commercial shipping posed a security problem and reproduce a lengthy National Federation of American Shipping letter opposing rapid restoration of Japan’s prewar four-million-ton fleet, particularly for long-distance international trade, on strategic, economic, competitive, and historical grounds.

subfiles.title: Memorandum recommending revised policy on Japanese merchant-ship reparations
subfiles.about: Recommends approving a revised U.S. position on Japanese merchant ships and seeking the Maritime Commission’s opinion while proceeding with SANACC submission.
subfiles.summary: Memo recommends the US disclaim its ship-reparations share, since only about eleven vessels remain available.

subfiles.title: Saltzman letter requesting Maritime Commission views
subfiles.about: Requests the Maritime Commission chairman’s opinion on a proposed U.S. policy concerning reparations claims to Japanese merchant shipping.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman asks the Maritime Commission for its view on the US ship-reparations proposal.

subfiles.title: Memorandum submitting Japanese shipping paper to SANACC
subfiles.from: Charles E. Saltzman, State Department member of SANACC
subfiles.about: Requests referral of the proposed Japanese merchant-shipping policy paper to SANACC’s Far Eastern Subcommittee.
subfiles.summary: Memo asks SANACC's Far Eastern Subcommittee to study the Japanese ship-reparations proposal.

subfiles.title: Draft U.S. position on reparations claims to Japanese merchant shipping
subfiles.about: Proposes that the United States renounce any share of Japanese merchant vessels and cease advocating a particular formula for distributing them.
subfiles.summary: The draft recommends rescinding the earlier SWNCC formula that allocated vessels according to proven wartime shipping losses and instructing the U.S. representative on the Far Eastern Commission to follow the majority view of other members. Appendix A reproduces the differing American, Chinese, French, Indian, Canadian, and British proposals, demonstrating disagreement over eligible losses, gross-tonnage ratios, vessel types, and whether European-war losses should count. Appendix B argues that the expected pool—no more than about eleven ships and 100,000 gross tons—was too small to aid favored countries or satisfy non-FEC claims and was therefore not worth a prolonged dispute. It also preserves SCAP’s authority to retain vessels temporarily for occupation needs and stresses that the proposed flexibility would not alter the total tonnage available as reparations.

subfiles.title: Estimate of Japanese vessels becoming available for reparations
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State; prepared by Selma Kallis
subfiles.about: Estimates the number and tonnage of Japanese ships meeting the proposed reparations threshold of more than 6,000 gross tons and over 15 knots.
subfiles.summary: Estimate lists nine Japanese vessels, 77,773 tons, potentially available for reparations, naming each ship.

subfiles.title: Memorandum submitting Japanese shipping paper to SWNCC
subfiles.from: Charles E. Saltzman, State Department member of SWNCC
subfiles.about: Requests referral of the proposed Japanese merchant-shipping paper to SWNCC’s Far Eastern Subcommittee.
subfiles.summary: Earlier SWNCC memo asks its Far Eastern Subcommittee to study the Japanese ship-reparations proposal.

subfiles.title: Saltzman letter to Smith on proposed SWNCC policy
subfiles.about: Solicits the Maritime Commission’s opinion on the conclusions of a State Department paper intended for SWNCC.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman sends Smith the SWNCC version of the proposed Japanese ship-reparations policy and vessel estimate.

subfiles.title: Kallis routing memorandum concerning SWNCC paper and letter
subfiles.about: Asks to be notified when the attached SWNCC paper and letter leave the Assistant Secretary’s office.
subfiles.summary: Routing note logs internal handling of the SWNCC ship-reparations paper and letter.

subfiles.title: Whitman memorandum forwarding draft SWNCC shipping paper
subfiles.about: Explains the purpose, departmental clearance, and Maritime Commission consultation behind the draft Japanese-shipping policy paper.
subfiles.summary: Whitman forwards a draft SWNCC shipping paper, cleared informally but recommended for Maritime Commission review.

subfiles.title: Keyes memorandum on the security aspects of Japanese shipping
subfiles.about: Forwards revised material and summarizes advice on whether Japanese commercial shipping presented a security problem.
subfiles.summary: Keyes reports the Army and Navy see no security concern in Japanese ship size or speed, unlike a British security objection.

subfiles.title: National Federation of American Shipping letter opposing rapid restoration of Japan’s merchant fleet
subfiles.from: Frazer A. Bailey, National Federation of American Shipping
subfiles.to: William H. Draper Jr., Assistant Secretary of the Army
subfiles.about: Argues against immediately rebuilding Japan’s merchant fleet to its 1930–1934 level or permitting extensive Japanese participation in long-distance international trades.
subfiles.summary: Speaking for owners of roughly two-thirds of privately owned American-flag ships, Bailey argues that Japanese recovery policy must account for its effects on the U.S. merchant marine and Allied economies. The letter disputes claims that shipping income was essential to Japan’s balance of payments, citing figures showing that it supplied under one percent of Japanese national income, and reviews Japan’s history of direct and indirect shipping subsidies. It questions using prewar production, trade, and fleet statistics as guides under Japan’s new political and economic order, contending that fleet growth should follow demonstrated industrial recovery and export demand. Its concluding recommendations favor restricting Japanese ships largely to domestic and nearby Asian trades, avoiding premature restoration of a four-million-gross-ton fleet, and giving American shipowners further opportunity to present their case.

interest: Shows postwar US debate over Japanese merchant-ship reparations, balanced against shipowners' push to limit Japan's maritime recovery.
